professor: Prof. Chen: Supporters of free markets say prices coordinate millions of decisions better than any planner, while critics worry about what markets leave undone. This debate shapes policies on trade, regulation and public spending. Do you agree that governments should unleash the free market? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Hannah: In a free market, prices come from millions of voluntary deals between buyers and sellers. Those prices carry useful information: when something becomes scarce, its price rises and producers respond quickly. No planner could collect and react to that information as efficiently, so supply and demand match more closely.
studentB: Leo: Markets rarely pay for basic research, because it may never lead to a product that sells. Yet that kind of research, which explains how the world works, is what makes later innovation possible. Without public funding, a purely free market would leave out the discoveries that new technologies depend on.

professor: Dr. Larsen: Many countries debate whether universities should limit admissions and become more selective. Supporters want degrees to keep their value, while critics point to the skills and opportunities a degree gives. Do you agree that university education should be capped and more selective? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Priya: When too many people hold a degree, each degree is worth less to employers, much like a market with too many diamonds. Limiting places would keep qualifications meaningful and help employers tell strong candidates apart. A more selective system could protect the value of a university education for everyone.
studentB: Victor: Most degrees teach skills that employers value, even when the subject is not directly related to the job. Students learn to meet deadlines, communicate clearly, work in teams and study independently. Capping places would shut many people out of those benefits, so I would rather improve courses than limit access.

professor: Dr. Kim: News outlets decide which stories to cover and how to frame them, and critics say this can distort how we see risks. Defenders say a free press must be allowed to choose. Do you agree that selective media coverage makes social problems worse? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Chloe: Media often take a worst-case quote from an expert and make it the headline. During outbreaks of illnesses like bird flu, 'it could become a pandemic' was presented as if it were certain. That kind of coverage creates panic that the evidence does not justify, and it can make real problems harder to manage.
studentB: Noah: Even if coverage is uneven, a free press must be allowed to choose what it reports. Freedom of expression is a core part of an open society, and limiting it would be more dangerous than occasional bias. People can compare several sources and decide for themselves what to believe.

professor: Prof. Weber: Digital rights management, or DRM, is software that limits how people can copy and use digital media. Companies say it protects their work, while users say it blocks reasonable uses. Do you agree that DRM unfairly restricts legitimate use of digital content? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Ana: DRM can get in the way of normal, legitimate use. Companies with thousands of computers often have to install licensed software one machine at a time, which costs them a lot of time and money. Copy protection treats honest customers like suspects and makes everyday work harder than it should be.
studentB: Tomas: Companies have the right to protect what they make, just like any other product. Copying media for other people is not the same as personal use, and the law should treat it the same way whoever does it. DRM is a reasonable way to enforce that rule.

professor: Dr. Flores: Some people propose a very high inheritance tax, even 100 percent, to reduce inherited wealth. Supporters see fairness and economic benefits, while critics see an attack on family and effort. What are the main advantages and disadvantages of this idea, and what is your overall judgement?
studentA: Hannah: If people knew their savings would be taxed away instead of passing to their children, they would have less reason to hoard money. They would be more likely to spend it, and that spending would support businesses, jobs and the wider economy during their lifetime.
studentB: Raul: People have a right to pass on what they earned through hard work. A tax of 100 percent treats a lifetime of effort as if it did not belong to the family, and it is hard to justify morally when even much lower rates already feel like a heavy burden.

professor: Prof. Lindqvist: Mobile phones are now common among school-age children, and parents are divided about it. Some see a useful tool for safety and contact, others see a distraction. Do you agree that children should have their own mobile phones? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Emma: Phones are part of everyday life, and cost need not be a problem. Parents can say no or set limits, and prepaid plans let children use a fixed amount of credit for calls and texts. With clear rules, a phone can teach responsibility instead of encouraging overspending.
studentB: Noah: Phones distract children from the people around them. Constant texting and gaming take the place of real conversation, so young people may grow up less able to talk face to face or to use good manners. I think children should wait until they are older.

professor: Dr. Brooks: Strikes by transport workers can stop commuters, goods and fuel from moving, which is why some governments want to restrict them. Others say strikes are a basic bargaining tool. What are the main advantages and disadvantages of this idea, and what is your overall judgement?
studentA: Nina: A ban would protect supplies. When transport stops, goods become scarce and prices rise, and isolated areas can run short of food or fuel. Keeping transport running means hospitals, shops and families are not harmed by a dispute they have no part in.
studentB: Raul: Banning strikes removes workers' strongest source of bargaining power. Even if arbitration is offered, employers have less reason to take workers' demands seriously when there is no credible threat behind them. Over time, pay and safety conditions could get worse.

professor: Dr. Santos: Some people argue that universities should publish everything they produce, from research papers to recorded lectures, for free. Others worry about the cost. What are the main advantages and disadvantages of this idea, and what is your overall judgement?
studentA: Marta: Higher education should be open to everyone. Universities are respected for their knowledge, so it is only fair that anyone can read their research and watch their lectures, not just people who can afford to enrol. Free access lets more people learn and builds public trust.
studentB: Ahmed: If everything is free to access, universities may lose private funding. Companies that want research for profit should pay for it themselves, but if the results are public, they have less reason to invest. That could leave universities and governments carrying more of the cost.

professor: Dr. Haddad: Housework and childcare keep families running, yet they are usually unpaid. Some people believe homemakers should receive a wage, while others disagree. What are the main advantages and disadvantages of paying people for this work, and what is your overall judgement?
studentA: Grace: A wage would recognise how valuable this work is. In an economy where value is measured in money, unpaid work looks like it has no worth. Paying homemakers would show that cooking, cleaning and caring for children are real contributions that society depends on.
studentB: Noah: One drawback is that family care is voluntary by nature. We do not pay people who volunteer for charities, even though that work can be demanding and skilled. Choosing to build a household implies accepting its tasks, so making them a paid job could change what family means.

professor: Prof. Costa: School is compulsory in most countries, but some people argue that attendance should be a choice. Supporters talk about cost and motivation, while critics worry about planning and fairness. What are the main advantages and disadvantages of making school attendance voluntary, and what is your overall judgement?
studentA: Mia: One advantage is that money would be used better. Schools and teachers are expensive, and spending on students who do not want to learn is wasted. Those students can also disrupt lessons, so removing them would make school easier for classmates who are ready to study.
studentB: Oscar: The main risk is planning. Governments set education budgets based on how many students attend. If attendance were voluntary, nobody could predict the numbers, so some schools might waste money on empty classrooms while others would not have enough teachers or space.

professor: Dr. Patel: Many social networks set a minimum age, yet lots of children are already online. Some parents allow accounts and supervise them closely, while others worry about the risks. What are the main advantages and disadvantages of letting children have social media accounts, and what is your overall judgement?
studentA: Priya: A big advantage is that parents can stay involved. They can set up the account themselves, use the privacy settings, and see everything their child posts or receives. That way the child learns to use the platform safely under supervision instead of discovering it alone.
studentB: Kenji: The danger is that children can be contacted by strangers. Many kids already have accounts, and people with bad intentions know it. A child updates the profile alone, so a parent cannot always see who is talking to them or what is being said.

professor: Prof. Nakamura: Tourism is one of the largest industries in the world, and many governments invest heavily in attracting visitors. People care because it can bring jobs and income, but it can also change local communities. Do you agree that tourism benefits a country? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Maya: I think tourism is good for a country. Visitors spend money on hotels, food and souvenirs, and they also pay taxes through their purchases. That money supports local businesses and creates a bigger market than residents alone could provide, so more people can find steady work.
studentB: Tyler: I am not convinced. Many hotels belong to large international chains that hire local staff mainly because labour is cheap. Small local hotels struggle to get loans because banks see them as risky, so much of the profit leaves the area and local people see little benefit.

professor: Dr. Kim: Many governments pay farmers subsidies and protect them with price supports and tariffs. Supporters say this keeps farms alive, while critics say it distorts the market. What are the main advantages and disadvantages of abolishing agricultural subsidies, and what is your overall judgement?
studentA: Tara: Ending subsidies would make farming fairer and more consistent with free trade. Today, prices, regulations and tariffs shape the sector so strongly that it behaves almost like a planned economy. Removing them would let farmers compete on quality and efficiency instead of political support.
studentB: Hugo: The risk is for small farmers, who often rely on government support for a large part of their income. Without it, many family farms would close, which could devastate rural communities. Reforming the system to make it fairer would be better than removing it completely.

professor: Dr. Ferreira: Cities spend huge amounts of money to host the Olympic Games, and the debate continues long after the closing ceremony. Supporters point to pride and tourism, while critics question the cost. Do you agree that hosting the Olympics is worth it? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Chloe: I think it is worth it. Big international events create a feel-good factor that is hard to put a price on. The whole country shares the excitement, people feel proud and united, and that mood can last for years after the games are over.
studentB: Leo: I disagree. Even though the games are a national event, the benefits mostly stay in the host city. In big countries, people far away see almost no new jobs, investment or infrastructure, yet everyone helps pay the bill through taxes.

professor: Prof. Reyes: Fish farming now supplies a large share of the seafood we eat, but it also raises environmental questions. Some people want strict limits, while others see it as a way to protect wild stocks and support rural jobs. Do you agree that fish farming should be banned or severely restricted? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Sara: Yes, it should be restricted. Fish kept in crowded sea cages can pass diseases and parasites to wild fish swimming nearby. The waste from a large farm also pollutes the surrounding water, so the damage spreads well beyond the farm and hurts the whole ecosystem.
studentB: Oscar: I disagree. Some people dislike how fish farms look, but that is a minor concern. Farms provide large amounts of sustainable fish and offer jobs in rural areas, which often have few other options. Those benefits are worth more than a slightly worse view.

professor: Prof. Costa: Cities keep growing as people move there for work, and housing is often expensive and scarce. Some planners favour tall apartment buildings, while others prefer lower buildings spread over a larger area. Do you agree that cities should build high-rises for housing? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Chloe: I agree. When many people move to a city looking for work, there is a shortage of affordable homes. High-rises fit many families on a small piece of land, which reduces urban sprawl and keeps transport links shorter and cheaper.
studentB: Noah: I am not sure. High-rise housing often carries a stigma, and that makes it less attractive on the property market. Even if the apartments are comfortable, buyers may link them with poorer areas, so the buildings can lose value and become harder to sell or rent.

professor: Prof. Costa: Many fast food restaurants include a small toy with children's meals, and health experts worry about the effect of this kind of marketing. Some places have considered banning the practice, while others prefer voluntary changes. Do you agree that selling toys with fast food meals should be prohibited? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Sofia: I agree with a ban. Young children cannot judge what calories, salt or saturated fat do to their bodies. A toy makes the meal more exciting than the food itself, so this marketing pushes kids towards unhealthy choices they cannot properly evaluate.
studentB: Alex: A ban would not achieve much. Companies are good at finding ways around the rules, for example by selling the toy separately. If the goal is healthier eating, it works better to pressure restaurants to improve their menus, as happened when one chain added fruit.

professor: Prof. Dubois: Many universities use standardized exams to compare thousands of applicants, but critics say these tests are unfair. Some people want to abolish them completely. Do you agree that standardized tests should no longer be used for university admission? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Julia: I think we should abolish them. When huge numbers of students take the same test, the scoring scale turns tiny differences in performance into big gaps in scores. A few extra questions right can decide who gets a place, which does not reflect real ability.
studentB: Ian: I disagree. Tests do favour wealthier students, but so does almost everything else universities could look at instead. Richer families have more educated parents, more books and better computers. Dropping the test would not remove that advantage, so we would lose a common measure for nothing.

professor: Prof. Lindqvist: Fast food advertising is everywhere, especially on television, and governments keep discussing whether it should be restricted. Some people worry about health, others about personal responsibility. What are the main advantages and disadvantages of banning it, and what is your overall judgement?
studentA: Paula: A ban would protect our health. Fast food is high in salt and sugar, and these tend to make food particles stick to the teeth, which leads to cavities. Less advertising would mean fewer people, especially children, getting used to eating this food all the time.
studentB: Noah: I see a risk of blaming the wrong target. Parents are the ones in charge, and children would eat less fast food if adults spent more time with them instead of using the television as a babysitter. A ban would treat the symptom, not the cause of childhood obesity.

professor: Dr. Ferreira: Large corporations shape the economy, politics and our daily lives, and people disagree strongly about how much power they should have. Some see them as engines of prosperity, others as a danger. Do you agree that corporations are a threat to democracy and society? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Mia: Yes, they are a threat. A company exists to make money and has no natural sense of empathy or responsibility. If profit is the only goal, it can ignore the damage it causes to people and the environment, so citizens need real power to keep corporations under control.
studentB: Leo: No, I think they are useful. Free trade existed long before corporations. What corporations added was limited liability, so investors could risk money without losing everything if the business failed. That encourages investment, creates jobs and supports the living standards that a healthy democracy needs.

professor: Dr. Larsen: Many people post online without using their real name, and lawmakers are asked whether this should be protected by law. Supporters talk about safety, critics about accountability. What are the main advantages and disadvantages of protecting online anonymity, and what is your overall judgement?
studentA: Sara: Anonymity lets people share the truth without risking their careers. Whistleblowers are a good example. Employees who know first-hand that their company is doing something illegal or immoral may stay silent if they fear being identified and punished.
studentB: Noah: A special legal protection may not be necessary. People have been able to use their right to free speech for years without hiding who they are. If anonymity is not essential to speak freely, then protecting it by law gives little benefit and may encourage careless behaviour.

professor: Prof. Lindqvist: Energy prices and climate concerns have pushed many countries to look at wind power as part of the answer. Supporters like its flexibility, while others doubt that it works everywhere. Do you agree that wind farms are a good solution to the energy crisis? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Emma: Yes, because wind power is scalable. Unlike traditional power plants, it can be generated on a small scale, so households, offices and small businesses could have their own turbines. With more research they could become cheap enough for ordinary buyers.
studentB: Ben: I am not convinced. A small turbine only works well in the right spot, and finding it requires a lot of research. Many homes simply do not get enough wind, so a turbine there would produce too little power. The idea sounds flexible but is limited in practice.

professor: Dr. Flores: Teachers give homework to extend learning beyond the school day, but many students and parents say it causes stress. Some people would like to ban it altogether. What are the main advantages and disadvantages of banning homework, and what is your overall judgement?
studentA: Leila: Banning homework would reduce stress. Many children find it boring and tiring, and teachers often underestimate how long a task takes. If something was not explained well in class, the homework can even be impossible, and that makes students dislike learning.
studentB: Ben: Homework is a valuable part of education. A school day has only a few hours, which is not enough to cover every subject properly. Homework extends study beyond school hours and allows children to learn more things in greater depth, so banning it would limit their education.

professor: Dr. Ivanova: Parents who can afford it often send their children to private schools, and some people think the law should limit this option. Others see it as a basic right. What are the main advantages and disadvantages of allowing private education, and what is your overall judgement?
studentA: Maya: Private schools can actually help state schools. Parents who use them still pay taxes, so that money is shared among fewer state-school pupils. This means there is more money per child in the state sector than if private education did not exist.
studentB: Raul: The supposed benefit is often exaggerated. Research suggests private schools do not necessarily teach better than state schools. Their pupils simply tend to be the kind of students who would do well anywhere, so families may pay a lot for an advantage that is not real.

professor: Prof. Costa: Few companies have equal numbers of men and women in their top leadership, and some countries have discussed legal quotas for boards of directors. Opinions are divided. What are the main advantages and disadvantages of a quota for women on corporate boards, and what is your overall judgement?
studentA: Hana: A quota could fix a clear imbalance. Women make up only a small share of board members at large companies, so they are heavily underrepresented at the highest levels of the economy. A fixed target would force companies to look at talented women they might otherwise overlook.
studentB: Adam: The main risk is uncertainty. Some companies already embrace hiring quotas as part of their culture, but we cannot predict how a legal requirement would affect performance across many different industries. It would be careless to assume the results would be positive everywhere.

professor: Dr. Haddad: Creative Commons licences allow other people to reuse and build on a creative work. Some argue that any project paid for with public or institutional money should have to use them. Do you agree that funding should depend on this? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Hana: I agree. Creative Commons lets others use existing work as a building block. A project can keep its value after the funding runs out, and other people can adapt it for new uses that the original creators never imagined. Funders should encourage that kind of openness.
studentB: Marcus: I disagree. Releasing work openly can be a good business decision, but it should be the creator's choice, not a condition for getting funds. Some creators will gain recognition and income by sharing, while others will lose both, and a forced rule would not suit them all.

professor: Prof. Novak: People live longer than in the past, and governments are under pressure to pay for pensions and healthcare. Some propose that everyone should work until a later age. What are the main advantages and disadvantages of raising the retirement age, and what is your overall judgement?
studentA: Isabel: A higher retirement age would help the economy. If people retire too early, the country loses productive workers and national prosperity falls. With an ageing population, the state cannot keep paying for pensions and healthcare without raising taxes to a very high level.
studentB: Noah: Quality of life matters as much as money. Many pensioners now expect to enjoy a good life after work, and it is unfair that people should spend almost all of their healthy years working. They deserve time to relax and benefit from better healthcare.

professor: Dr. Ferreira: Some economists suggest a very small tax on currency trading, known as a Tobin tax, to raise money for global needs such as development aid. Supporters and critics disagree about its effects. Do you agree that this tax is a good idea? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Paula: A small tax on currency trading could raise a huge amount of money each year. Even a cautious estimate would be comparable to what rich countries currently give in official aid, so it could fund real help without hurting ordinary taxpayers.
studentB: Hugo: I disagree. Large sums of aid money can create a moral hazard, because governments get used to international institutions solving their problems for them. Over time, they may never build the efficient economies they need to stand on their own.

professor: Prof. Nakamura: Many students already spend hours on social media, so some schools wonder whether it should be taught as part of the curriculum. People care because it affects both learning and wellbeing. What do you see as the main advantages and disadvantages, and what is your overall judgement?
studentA: Sofia: Social media can be a useful classroom tool. Students can discuss lessons with classmates and with pupils in other schools, share their work instantly, and receive reminders about homework and exam dates from teachers without any delay.
studentB: Noah: The main risk is distraction. School is meant to prepare students for professional life, and in most offices personal social media is discouraged or blocked so people can concentrate. Using it in class could weaken that habit of focus.

professor: Dr. Haddad: People often say that a university degree is the safest route to a good life, yet some famous business leaders never finished college. This question matters to anyone choosing a career path. Do you agree that academic qualifications ensure success in life? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Paula: I think they do help a lot. A university education exposes you to people from different backgrounds and makes you think about culture and values. Those experiences shape a well-rounded person, and that is a big part of being successful overall.
studentB: Alex: Not necessarily. Many successful people have no degree at all, and some of the best known entrepreneurs started companies without finishing college. Many qualified professionals even end up working for them, so a diploma clearly does not guarantee success.

professor: Dr. Santos: Many low-income countries rely on visitors to bring in money, but tourism can change the places people come to see. It is a question for both economists and local communities. Do you agree that tourism is a good development strategy for poor countries? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Nina: I agree, if it is managed carefully. Tourism and conservation can work together, and ecotourism shows that visitors can even help monitor and protect the natural areas and historical sites they come to see, while local people earn an income.
studentB: Daniel: I do not think it is that simple. Tourists can damage more than ecosystems and historic sites. Large numbers of visitors can disturb the daily routines and traditions of local communities, and that can change the way of life in a place permanently.

professor: Prof. Lindqvist: Children see a huge amount of advertising on television and online, and some countries limit how companies can target them. People care because young viewers may not understand that ads are trying to sell something. Do you agree that advertising aimed at children should be restricted? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Lucia: Yes. Today children can choose from public, commercial and subscription channels, so limits on advertising will not threaten broadcasters. Commercial channels can still earn revenue and offer good children's programmes, and many countries already have similar rules.
studentB: Oscar: I disagree. Children also watch programmes that adults enjoy, and some adults are also easy to influence. If we restrict ads for children, where do we stop? Children see advertising on radio, in cinemas, online and on street billboards too.

professor: Prof. Chen: Many teenagers want to earn their own money while they are still at school, and some families see a job as useful experience. Others think it distracts from studying. Do you agree that high school students should have part-time jobs? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Hannah: I think school should come first. Students are in full-time education and need good grades for university and their future careers. A part-time job takes time and energy, and that can make it harder to concentrate on their studies.
studentB: Ahmed: I disagree, because a job can actually help students. Work experience makes them think about their future careers, and it can motivate them to work hard for good grades so that they can get better jobs and keep studying later.

professor: Dr. Okafor: Mobile phones and the internet are spreading quickly across Africa, and many people expect young entrepreneurs to benefit. Others doubt that technology alone changes much. Do you agree that new technologies will turn Africa's young people into entrepreneurs? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Sara: Yes, I think so. Mobile phones let young people connect with each other and with customers, share ideas and build solutions to local problems. With cheap devices spreading quickly across the region, many can start businesses with very little capital.
studentB: Kevin: I am not convinced. The people who succeed usually already have connections, access to credit, reliable electricity and free time to develop their idea. Technology is often created by those wealthy entrepreneurs, so it does not automatically create new ones.

professor: Dr. Flores: Women's sport usually gets far less television and news coverage than men's sport, and some people think laws should change that. Others prefer to let the market decide. Do you agree that the media should be forced to cover women's and men's sport equally? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Marta: Yes. The media decides what counts as newsworthy, and public opinion follows. Sports that get a lot of coverage seem important, so equal coverage would show young people that women's competitions deserve the same attention and respect.
studentB: Hugo: I disagree. Female athletes already get a lot of attention at events such as the Olympic Games and tennis tournaments, so girls already have plenty of role models. More coverage would be welcome, but it should not be forced on the media.

professor: Prof. Nakamura: Most academic research is published in a few major languages, which makes it hard for researchers in other regions to read. Some people suggest subsidising translations into the languages of developing countries. What are the main advantages and disadvantages of this idea, and what is your overall judgement?
studentA: Leila: Rich countries can afford to translate whatever research they find interesting, but universities in poorer regions have far fewer resources. Subsidised translation would let their researchers read and take part in the global conversation, instead of watching from outside.
studentB: Oscar: The main risk is cost. Translating everything is prohibitively expensive, and no programme could cover every language. Money spent on translation could be taken away from other priorities such as laboratories, salaries or scholarships.

professor: Prof. Weber: Websites and apps collect data about our age, location and habits so that advertisers can show us targeted ads. Some people want to ban this practice, while companies say it is useful. What are the main advantages and disadvantages of a ban, and what is your overall judgement?
studentA: Hana: A ban would help protect fairness. Targeting individuals lets companies charge different people different prices and show them different offers based on their data, which can undermine fair competition and treat customers unequally.
studentB: Ahmed: A ban would make advertising less efficient. Targeting lets companies reach the right audience instead of showing ads to everyone at random, and that especially helps small businesses and niche markets that cannot afford mass advertising.

professor: Dr. Flores: Sport is a huge part of life in most countries, from school games to professional leagues, and people generally assume it is good for us. Still, not everyone has the same experience. Do you agree that sports are really good for us? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Leila: Yes, I do. Sport gives young people role models to follow. This matters especially for those from poor backgrounds, who can see athletes who escaped difficult situations through hard work and talent, and it gives them hope.
studentB: Jake: Not always. Sport teaches lessons, but not all of them are positive. Children who are not naturally talented often experience failure and embarrassment, which can damage their confidence and even put them off exercise for life.

professor: Dr. Flores: Many schools offer clubs, sports and other activities in addition to normal lessons. Supporters say these build useful skills, but others worry about time. Do you agree that schools should place strong emphasis on co-curricular activities? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Hana: Yes. A wide range of experiences prepares people for an uncertain future. Many people change careers several times in their lives, so the broad education that activities outside lessons provide is better preparation than study alone.
studentB: Victor: I disagree. Academic education should not be compromised by too much emphasis on other activities. Specialist professions usually offer several career options anyway, and even someone who is forced to leave a field can often continue in a different role.

professor: Prof. Lindqvist: Some governments limit how much foreign investors can put into their economy, hoping to protect local businesses and avoid financial bubbles. Critics say it harms growth and relations with other countries. Do you agree with limiting foreign investment? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Leila: Yes. A cap on foreign investment makes a bubble economy less likely. It also encourages local investors to put their money into the home economy, where prices are likely to be lower because less outside money is competing for assets.
studentB: Alex: I disagree. Economies are becoming more connected, so trade barriers are both impractical and undesirable. Other countries may take offence and respond with economic or diplomatic measures, which would leave the country more isolated than before.

professor: Prof. Costa: Let's talk about climate policy. Governments can cut carbon emissions either with a cap-and-trade system, where companies trade emission permits, or with a carbon tax on every ton. People care because the choice affects costs for business and consumers. Do you agree that cap-and-trade is preferable? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Emma: Imagine two power plants. One can cut emissions cheaply, the other only at a high cost. With cap-and-trade, the cheap plant cuts more and sells its spare permits. The country reaches its target at a lower total cost than if everyone had to pay the same tax.
studentB: Ryan: I prefer a carbon tax because cap-and-trade is complicated. It needs a permit market, careful monitoring and strict rules, and companies can find ways to game the system. A tax is simple to understand, easy to apply and gives businesses a clear price to plan around.

professor: Prof. Alvarez: Some people argue that studying should be compulsory until the end of a university degree, not just school. Supporters see it as a way to prepare everyone for the future, while others see it as too strict. What are the main advantages and disadvantages of this idea, and what is your overall judgement?
studentA: Elena: A society benefits when all its young people are educated. If studies are compulsory, nobody is left behind because of money or background, and the country gets a better trained workforce. Education becomes a shared responsibility, not a private choice.
studentB: Noah: Adults over eighteen are not children. They know their own interests and should choose their own path, whether that is work, travel or starting a business. Forcing someone to study something they don't want can waste time and money and make them resent learning.

professor: Dr. Larsen: Many governments require, or are considering, clear labels on food packaging to help people eat more healthily. Supporters think better information leads to better choices, but others have doubts. What are the main advantages and disadvantages of this idea, and what is your overall judgement?
studentA: Ana: Clear labels protect consumers. They let shoppers see what they are really buying, compare products quickly and avoid ingredients or amounts of sugar and salt that they want to limit. Companies also feel pressure to improve recipes when everything is visible.
studentB: Peter: A drawback is that companies can use label design to mislead. Once a symbol looks healthy, brands copy its style to make a product seem better than it is. A yogurt can be marketed as health food with convincing packaging even when it contains a lot of sugar.

professor: Prof. Reyes: Today it is hard to apply for a job, study or use public services without going online. Some people therefore say internet access should be a basic human right, while others disagree. Do you agree that internet access is a human right? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Marta: I don't think it is a right in itself. The internet is useful, but it is a tool that helps us exercise real rights, like getting information. Someone locked in a library with no internet could still read and learn, so their right to information would not be lost.
studentB: Kevin: I think it is. Nowadays information, jobs, banking and education all depend on being online. People without access are excluded from basic parts of modern life, so the right to access information now includes a connection that lets them use it.

professor: Dr. Larsen: Many students and parents spend a lot of time and money choosing the right university. Some people say the name on the diploma opens doors, while others say that what you actually learn matters more. Does it matter where you go to university? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Marta: I think skills matter more than the name. University should not be like collecting badges. What counts is what you learn there and how you use it. If different universities teach skills of very different quality, that is a problem with the education system itself.
studentB: Tomas: I think it does matter. Well-known universities impress employers and open doors, especially early in a career. A strong degree from a respected institution gives graduates a better chance of getting a good job or being accepted into further studies.

professor: Dr. Singh: In many countries, teachers' salaries mostly depend on how many years they have worked. Some people want to change this and link pay to performance, as many companies do. Do you agree that teachers should be paid based on merit? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Laura: Seniority-based pay gives teachers little reason to keep improving, however motivated they were at the start. If good results led to better pay, teachers would have a clear incentive to develop their skills and try new methods, and students would benefit.
studentB: Adam: The idea is hard to apply fairly. Test scores depend on many things besides the teacher, such as family background and class size. Tests also measure only part of good teaching, so merit pay could reward the wrong things and create unfair competition between colleagues.

professor: Prof. Adeyemi: Some people propose replacing income tax with a tax on spending, such as sales tax. Supporters say it would simplify the system and make goods cheaper, while critics see practical problems. What are the main advantages and disadvantages of this idea, and what is your overall judgement?
studentA: Paula: Without income tax, employers pay less in taxes and social costs, so the price of goods can fall. Think of a car: a large part of its price includes tax on the wages of everyone involved in making it. Removing that tax could make products cheaper.
studentB: Daniel: A tax on spending can be hard to manage, especially if rates differ by product. Someone has to decide what counts as a luxury, and owners of those goods would lobby the government to be classified differently. The system could become complicated and unfair.

professor: Dr. Patel: Hosting the Olympic Games is a huge project that attracts attention from all over the world. Some countries want to host them, while others worry about the cost. Consider a country like South Africa. What are the main advantages and disadvantages of hosting, and what is your overall judgement?
studentA: Alicia: Hosting a major sporting event brings economic benefits, such as tourism, jobs and investment in transport. The cost is high, but some cities already have suitable venues, which reduces the amount of new building needed and the overall expense.
studentB: Daniel: The benefits mostly stay in one city and one country. Some events must take place elsewhere. For example, a landlocked city cannot host sailing, so organizers need venues far away. The costs and the disruption can be spread out while the rewards are not.

professor: Dr. Santos: The euro is the shared currency of many European countries, which makes trade easier but also means they share one central bank. Some economists argue that countries should go back to their own currencies. Do you agree that the single currency should be abolished? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Alicia: Countries have different economies, so they need different monetary policies. A shared currency forces one policy on everyone, even when it suits some countries and hurts others. Having their own currencies would let governments respond to their own situation.
studentB: Adam: Abolishing the euro would be risky. Investors might move their money out of weaker countries before the change, causing capital flight and financial instability. Many banks and businesses made long-term plans around a shared currency, and unwinding it would be costly and chaotic.

professor: Dr. Brooks: Imagine universities everywhere competing to attract the best students, no matter where they come from. This could change how education works for both students and countries. What are the main advantages and disadvantages of this idea, and what is your overall judgement?
studentA: Leila: An international education helps produce global problem solvers. Students who study with people from other countries learn different perspectives, build networks and practice working across cultures, which are skills that employers value in a connected world.
studentB: Tyler: Governments want their own citizens to be competitive in the job market. If universities admit the best students from anywhere, local students may lose places or opportunities, and a country could end up with a weaker home-grown workforce.

professor: Prof. Weber: Scientists have warned about climate change for decades, and emissions are still rising. Some people believe it is already too late to prevent serious damage, while others think we can still make a difference. Do you agree that we are too late? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Grace: I think it may be too late. Fast-growing economies are increasing emissions quickly through fossil fuels and deforestation. Richer countries took hundreds of years to reach a living standard where environmental protection became a priority, so it is hard to ask others to slow down.
studentB: Kevin: I don't think it is too late. Wealthy countries have the money and technology to cut their emissions sharply. If they do, total emissions can stabilize even while some developing economies keep growing, and later technology can help those countries catch up cleanly.

professor: Prof. Novak: Some cities are thinking about banning private cars from their centers to reduce pollution and noise. Supporters say it would make cities more pleasant, but others see practical problems. What are the main advantages and disadvantages of this idea, and what is your overall judgement?
studentA: Alicia: Banning cars would encourage people to use public transport, which can be faster for commuters. Busy professionals can avoid traffic jams and parking problems, and they might even get some useful exercise by walking part of the way.
studentB: Sam: One problem is that traffic doesn't disappear. It moves to the edges of the city. People would have to go around the center to reach their destination, and congestion could get worse on the roads and highways surrounding the banned area.

professor: Prof. Weber: Some people suggest setting a legal maximum for salaries to reduce inequality, so that no one can earn more than a fixed amount. Supporters see it as fairer, but critics see risks for the economy. What are the main advantages and disadvantages of this idea, and what is your overall judgement?
studentA: Sara: Equality is a good thing in itself. A salary cap would narrow the gap between top earners and everyone else. It could also ease social tensions, which can build up when people feel that pay at the top is out of proportion.
studentB: Omar: Money is one of the most direct incentives. People respond to rewards, and high salaries encourage talented people to work hard. This can raise productivity and tax revenue, which governments can spend on public services, so a cap might hurt everyone.

professor: Dr. Ivanova: Supermarkets sometimes sell a few popular products below cost to attract shoppers, hoping people will buy other items too. These are called loss leaders. Some people want to ban the practice. Do you agree that retailers should be prohibited from doing this? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Tara: Selling at a loss is a strategy large retailers can afford and small shops cannot. It pushes smaller competitors out of business and leaves shoppers with fewer choices later. Banning it would protect competition and keep local shops alive.
studentB: Ahmed: I would not ban it. Loss leaders give shoppers cheap prices on everyday goods, which helps people on tight budgets. A ban would also be hard to enforce, because it is difficult to prove what a store paid for each item or why it set a price.

professor: Prof. Novak: Many countries require students to take physical education, and schools often debate whether it deserves a place in the timetable. Supporters point to health and sport, while critics point to personal choice. What are the main advantages and disadvantages of making PE compulsory, and what is your overall judgement?
studentA: Tara: One clear advantage is that school sport depends on full classes. If students could simply opt out, many teams would struggle to find enough players, and talented students might never discover their ability because they never got the chance to try.
studentB: Ben: A disadvantage is that compulsory PE takes away personal choice. Students already follow the curriculum the state sets, but being forced to exercise feels more personal, and some people believe they should decide for themselves what to do with their own bodies.

professor: Prof. Costa: Chess is played by millions of people around the world, yet it has never been part of the Olympic Games. Some argue that the Games would benefit from including it, while others think it does not belong there. Do you agree that chess should be introduced at the Olympics? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Grace: I think chess should be an Olympic sport. It has a huge number of players and national federations worldwide, but its fans are not represented at the biggest sporting event. It is also easy to follow as a spectator, so including it would make it even more popular.
studentB: Daniel: I disagree. Chess already has its own major tournaments, just like most other sports, and those events are built around what chess players need. The Olympics would add little for them, and the game may be better off keeping its own prestigious competitions.

professor: Dr. Haddad: History has been a standard school subject for generations, but some people question how useful it really is compared with science or vocational training. Others believe it shapes how young people think. Do you agree that history deserves a large place in the school curriculum? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Priya: I think school history is overrated. Lessons often focus on memorising names and dates, which rarely helps in real life. Students would gain more from spending that time on science and practical, job-related subjects that prepare them for work.
studentB: Tomas: I disagree. History teaches skills that matter in any career, such as thinking critically, building a reasoned argument and understanding other points of view. It also helps students understand their own culture and other cultures, which is valuable in a global economy.

professor: Dr. Brooks: Airport security can be slow and intrusive, so some governments consider giving extra checks to passengers whose behaviour or travel patterns look unusual. Supporters say this is more efficient, while critics doubt it works. Do you agree that airports should use security profiling? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Tara: I support profiling because the alternatives are worse. Scanning and patting down every traveller, including elderly or disabled people, is expensive, excessive and humiliating. Focusing attention on a smaller group would keep security high while making the process more dignified for most passengers.
studentB: Jake: I don't think profiling makes airports safer. Extra checks on a few suspicious travellers do not remove the need to screen everyone else properly. It would simply mean that people with unusual habits, like paying cash for a one-way ticket with no bags, get more attention.

professor: Dr. Haddad: In many countries, going to university has become the default path after school, and some people say fewer students should go. This could change how universities work and who gets access to them. What are the main advantages and disadvantages of encouraging fewer people to attend university, and what is your overall judgement?
studentA: Maya: An advantage is that universities could focus on real academic work. With fewer students, departments could give serious learners the resources, time and space they need, and students would be surrounded by peers who truly love their subject.
studentB: Greg: A risk is that university gives people a goal to aim for. Many families see it as the main route to better-paid jobs, especially low-income and minority families, so discouraging attendance could close that door and reduce social mobility.

professor: Dr. Rivera: Tourism is a major industry in many countries, including Tunisia, where beaches and historic sites attract visitors every year. Relying on it can bring jobs, but it also carries risks. What are the main advantages and disadvantages of a country depending on tourism for growth, and what is your overall judgement?
studentA: Lucia: A big advantage is employment. Tourism is one of the largest employers in Tunisia and creates a very large number of jobs. That matters a lot in a country with many university students who expect to find work after they graduate.
studentB: Raul: A disadvantage is that profit margins can be small, especially in the cheaper end of the market where visitors mainly pay for hotels and beaches. A country needs to offer higher-value experiences, such as cultural tourism, to earn more from each visitor.

professor: Prof. Moreau: Boarding schools, where students live on site during term, are a long tradition in some countries. Families choose them for the facilities and the structure, but some worry about the effects on children. Do you agree that boarding schools are beneficial to children? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Chloe: I think they are beneficial. Living at school gives children constant access to libraries, computers and teachers, even while they do their homework. That creates a strong learning environment that many children would not have at home.
studentB: Felix: I'm not convinced. Specialist boarding schools can focus too much on one subject or style and neglect everything else. They can also force children who love something like ballet or music to leave home when they would rather stay with their families.

professor: Prof. Adeyemi: Some parents believe in firm rules and high expectations, while others prefer a more relaxed style that leaves room for play. People care because parenting shapes confidence, habits and happiness later in life. Do you agree that strict parenting works best? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Hannah: I agree that strict parenting works best. Children enjoy the satisfaction of achieving something genuinely difficult after hours of practice. They can recover from failure, and that makes success feel greater, just as it does for adults.
studentB: Peter: I disagree, because children need to play. Play is more an attitude than a specific activity. A child can work very hard at a game or a hobby and still enjoy it, so pressure and strict rules are not needed to get effort.

professor: Prof. Dubois: More graduates now consider a Master's degree after their bachelor's, hoping to stand out in a crowded job market. It costs time and money, so the decision is not easy. Do you agree that graduates should get a Master's degree? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Isabel: Yes, I think it is worth it. A Master's helps you stand out when many candidates have the same first degree. It shows deeper knowledge, and a research Master's proves you can motivate yourself and deliver a project mostly on your own.
studentB: Daniel: Not always. In many fields, a year of real work experience is more useful than another year or two of study. Employers often value practical skills, and the extra cost of a Master's may not pay off unless it clearly leads to a specific career.

professor: Prof. Murphy: Governments in many countries give public money to theatres, museums and orchestras. Supporters say culture needs protection, while critics say taxpayers should not pay for it. Do you agree that arts subsidies should be abolished? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Leila: I agree. The arts do not have to depend on the state. Wealthy patrons have supported artists for centuries, and many companies are happy to sponsor cultural events because it links their brand with creativity and quality.
studentB: Victor: I disagree. Subsidies keep the arts affordable, which is crucial for education. Without them, schools and young people could not afford music lessons or visits to museums, galleries, plays and concerts, and they would miss the chance to enjoy their culture.

professor: Dr. Flores: Many governments offer unemployment benefits, and some have tried requiring recipients to do community work in return. Supporters say it builds work habits, while critics question whether it leads to real jobs. Do you think the unemployed should be made to work for their welfare money? Describe the main advantages and disadvantages, and give your overall judgement.
studentA: Isabel: One advantage is that people in these schemes show employers they are willing and able to work. They also gain skills and experience in a real workplace, which can change how employers see them and make it easier to find a proper job afterwards.
studentB: Sam: A big disadvantage is that these schemes do not create jobs. If companies simply are not hiring, forcing people to work for their benefits will not help them find employment. Most unemployment comes from weak demand for workers, not from people refusing to work.

professor: Dr. Kim: In many countries, millions of children still do not complete primary school. Some experts argue that the main problem is a lack of investment in teachers, while others point to different causes. Do you agree that this is the greatest barrier? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Alicia: Yes, I do. Schools in rural areas often have no teachers because nobody wants to move there. Better pay, bonuses and housing for teachers who relocate would put qualified people where children need them most, and that would keep more children in school.
studentB: Hugo: I would not say it is the greatest barrier. Money alone does not help if it is badly managed. Governments should invest in strong management and accountability so teachers are present, supported and used efficiently, and so public resources actually reach the classroom.

professor: Prof. Novak: Many children now ask for a mobile phone at a young age, and parents and schools are not sure what to do. Some see useful tools, others see a constant distraction. Should every child have a mobile phone? Describe the main advantages and disadvantages and give your overall judgement.
studentA: Emma: A phone can actually help children in school. They can set reminders to do their homework, and some studies suggest it can increase motivation. If children learn to use phones for useful things, they may even get better results.
studentB: Omar: The main risk is distraction. A phone makes it easy to lose concentration, and it can stop children from working properly, both in school and at home. Doing a task with a phone nearby makes mistakes more likely.

professor: Dr. Haddad: We see advertising everywhere, on our phones, on the street and on television. Some people say it informs us, while others say it pushes us to buy things we do not need. Do you agree that advertisements do more harm than good? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Sofia: I agree. Advertisers mainly want to make a profit, so they often promote products that are unhealthy. Fast food adverts aimed at children are a good example, and they are partly responsible for the growth in childhood obesity.
studentB: Kevin: I disagree. Advertising helps us choose between competing products by showing what is new. It tells us about computers with more powerful features, or foods with added vitamins. Without it, we would know much less about what is available.

professor: Dr. Singh: Climate change affects poorer regions such as parts of Africa more than richer ones. Wealthy countries are being asked to pay for adaptation, such as stronger flood defences and drought-resistant farming. Do you agree that the developed world should fund African climate adaptation? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Rosa: I agree. Wealthy countries have the money and the technology, and they have produced most of the emissions over time. It is fair that they help the places that suffer the most from the changes, even though those places contributed the least.
studentB: Ahmed: I am not sure it is the best use of money. Many adaptation methods are expensive compared with the benefits they bring. Aid should go where it can make the biggest difference, such as health or education, rather than into projects with a poor return.

professor: Dr. Patel: Governments sometimes set legal standards for energy efficiency and clean energy, rather than waiting for companies to improve voluntarily. People disagree about whether the market alone can deliver progress. Do you agree that we should not trust the market to improve energy standards? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Priya: I agree. Companies make money from the current system, so they have little reason to spend heavily on new technology without any push. Government standards give them a guaranteed market, and that makes the early investment worth the risk.
studentB: Hugo: I disagree. Governments cannot predict which technology will succeed, and trying to plan it in advance is risky. Companies that are free to respond to changing conditions usually find better solutions than rules written years before the technology exists.

professor: Dr. Larsen: Schools provide lockers for students to keep their belongings, but they are sometimes searched because of safety concerns. People are divided between school authority and student privacy. Do you agree that schools have the right to search students' lockers? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Elena: Yes, they do. Lockers are school property, and students only borrow them, much like sports equipment. Students should be told that searches are possible. Accepting that is part of belonging to a school community with rules and responsibilities.
studentB: Hugo: I disagree. Searching lockers when staff suspect one student can feel intrusive and unfair. Schools should focus on stopping dangerous items from coming in, for example with checks that apply equally to everybody instead of singling out particular students.

professor: Dr. Larsen: During financial crises, governments have sometimes used public money to rescue failing banks. Supporters say it prevents wider damage, while critics find it unfair. Describe the main advantages and disadvantages of governments bailing out banks, and give your overall judgement.
studentA: Priya: The main advantage is protecting ordinary people. Many pension plans and savings are invested in financial companies. If banks go bankrupt, those investments disappear, and retirees lose money. A rescue can keep major institutions running and limit the damage.
studentB: Tyler: A clear disadvantage is fairness. Money naturally moves from weak companies to successful ones. If the government taxes successful businesses to rescue those with a poor business model, it punishes good decisions and rewards poor ones.

professor: Dr. Larsen: Students in many countries spend hours on homework each week. Some teachers and parents believe it is essential, while others think it has little value. Do you agree that homework is a waste of time? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Mia: I partly agree. Homework takes a lot of time, not only at home but also in class, because the teacher has to explain the task and later go through and mark the answers. That time could be used for teaching something new.
studentB: Kenji: I disagree. Homework teaches students to take responsibility for their own learning. It is the same duty as classwork, except that at home nobody is watching you. Learning to work without supervision is a useful skill for later life.

professor: Prof. Costa: In football, it can be hard to see whether the ball completely crossed the goal line, and mistakes can decide important matches. Goal-line technology can settle this. Describe the main advantages and disadvantages of introducing it, and give your overall judgement.
studentA: Elena: Technology is already used in sports such as tennis, cricket and rugby, and it works well. Guaranteeing correct decisions has made a clear difference in many matches, so it has become a natural aid to the game.
studentB: Jake: The main problem is cost. Not every club can afford the equipment, so it would be limited to professional games. That creates a gap between wealthy competitions and local football, which does not fit the idea of a game open to everyone.

professor: Prof. Nakamura: Many countries give public money to elite athletes so they can train full-time and compete internationally. Others think this money should go elsewhere. Do you agree that taxpayers' money should be used to fund top sportspeople? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Hannah: Yes. Other nations invest public money in sport, so we have to do the same to keep up. Without state funding, our athletes would be at a disadvantage and success at international competitions would be much harder to achieve.
studentB: Tomas: I disagree. Public funding often means that taxes paid by poorer people end up supporting well-off athletes. Many funded sports, such as sailing or rowing, are mostly open to children from wealthy families, so the benefit is unequal.

professor: Prof. Reyes: Many countries set a legal minimum wage, a lowest hourly pay that employers must offer. Supporters say it protects workers, while critics say it can reduce hiring. Do you agree that there should be a national minimum wage? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Tara: Yes, I think so. Businesses are concerned with their bottom line, so many will pay as little as they can to increase profit. A legal minimum protects people with few options from being underpaid, even though some employers would pay fairly anyway.
studentB: Peter: I am not convinced. Without a fixed minimum, wages would reflect the real economic situation of the country, and more people could find work. An artificial floor can stop small businesses from hiring, especially people with little experience.
